{"arxiv_id":"2402.02456v2","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02456v2","title":"tnGPS: Discovering Unknown Tensor Network Structure Search Algorithms
  via Large Language Models (LLMs)","authors":["Junhua Zeng","Chao Li","Zhun Sun","Qibin Zhao","Guoxu Zhou"],"published_date":"2024-02-04T12:06:13Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"Tensor networks are efficient for extremely high-dimensional representation,
but their model selection, known as tensor network structure search (TN-SS), is
a challenging problem. Although several works have targeted TN-SS, most
existing algorithms are manually crafted heuristics with poor performance,
suffering from the curse of dimensionality and local convergence. In this work,
we jump out of the box, studying how to harness large language models (LLMs) to
automatically discover new TN-SS algorithms, replacing the involvement of human
experts. By observing how human experts innovate in research, we model their
common workflow and propose an automatic algorithm discovery framework called
tnGPS. The proposed framework is an elaborate prompting pipeline that instruct
LLMs to generate new TN-SS algorithms through iterative refinement and
enhancement. The experimental results demonstrate that the algorithms
discovered by tnGPS exhibit superior performance in benchmarks compared to the
current state-of-the-art methods.","github_url":"https://github.com/ChaoLiAtRIKEN/tngps","main_contributions":"The paper introduces tnGPS, an LLM-driven framework for automatically discovering novel and effective Tensor Network Structure Search (TN-SS) algorithms tailored to specific downstream tasks. It demonstrates that algorithms discovered by tnGPS outperform existing TN-SS algorithms on benchmark data.","methodology":"tnGPS uses a prompting pipeline to guide LLMs in generating new TN-SS algorithms through iterative refinement and enhancement, mimicking the innovation process of human experts. This involves knowledge categorization, recombination, incremental innovation, and diversity injection.","experimental_setup":"The effectiveness of tnGPS was evaluated on natural image compression (BSD500 dataset) and model compression for Gaussian processes (CCPP and MG datasets). Performance was compared against existing TN-SS algorithms like TNGA, TNLS, GREEDY, and TnALE using metrics like compression ratio and relative squared error (RSE). Ablation studies were conducted to assess the impact of individual components of tnGPS.","limitations":"The performance of the discovered algorithms is subject to variation due to changes in LLMs and the potential for unreliable results due to the hallucination issue.","future_research_directions":"Future research could focus on improving the reliability and practicality of LLMs in algorithm discovery, potentially by constructing more precise prompts to guide them effectively. Also, explore whether machines may eventually replace human expertise entirely."}

{"arxiv_id":"2402.14905v2","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14905v2","title":"MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter Language Models for
  On-Device Use Cases","authors":["Zechun Liu","Changsheng Zhao","Forrest Iandola","Chen Lai","Yuandong Tian","Igor Fedorov","Yunyang Xiong","Ernie Chang","Yangyang Shi","Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi","Liangzhen Lai","Vikas Chandra"],"published_date":"2024-02-22T18:58:55Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"This paper addresses the growing need for efficient large language models
(LLMs) on mobile devices, driven by increasing cloud costs and latency
concerns. We focus on designing top-quality LLMs with fewer than a billion
parameters, a practical choice for mobile deployment. Contrary to prevailing
belief emphasizing the pivotal role of data and parameter quantity in
determining model quality, our investigation underscores the significance of
model architecture for sub-billion scale LLMs. Leveraging deep and thin
architectures, coupled with embedding sharing and grouped-query attention
mechanisms, we establish a strong baseline network denoted as MobileLLM, which
attains a remarkable 2.7%/4.3% accuracy boost over preceding 125M/350M
state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we propose an immediate block-wise
weight-sharing approach with no increase in model size and only marginal
latency overhead. The resultant models, denoted as MobileLLM-LS, demonstrate a
further accuracy enhancement of 0.7%/0.8% than MobileLLM 125M/350M. Moreover,
MobileLLM model family shows significant improvements compared to previous
sub-billion models on chat benchmarks, and demonstrates close correctness to
LLaMA-v2 7B in API calling tasks, highlighting the capability of small models
for common on-device use cases.","github_url":"https://github.com/facebookresearch/MobileLLM","main_contributions":"This paper introduces MobileLLM, a family of sub-billion parameter language models optimized for on-device use. The key finding is that for small LLMs, model architecture, particularly depth, is more important than width. The paper also proposes immediate block-wise weight sharing (MobileLLM-LS) for further accuracy gains and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot tasks, question answering, reading comprehension, chat, and API calling compared to other sub-billion parameter models.","methodology":"The methodology involves designing deep and thin transformer architectures, revisiting embedding sharing methods, utilizing grouped query attention, and introducing immediate block-wise weight sharing. {"arxiv_id":"2402.05140v3","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05140v3","title":"Tag-LLM: Repurposing General-Purpose LLMs for Specialized Domains","authors":["Junhong Shen","Neil Tenenholtz","James Brian Hall","David Alvarez-Melis","Nicolo Fusi"],"published_date":"2024-02-06T20:11:54Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in
understanding and generating natural language. However, their capabilities wane
in highly specialized domains underrepresented in the pretraining corpus, such
as physical and biomedical sciences. This work explores how to repurpose
general LLMs into effective task solvers for specialized domains. We introduce
a novel, model-agnostic framework for learning custom input tags, which are
parameterized as continuous vectors appended to the LLM's embedding layer, to
condition the LLM. We design two types of input tags: domain tags are used to
delimit specialized representations (e.g., chemical formulas) and provide
domain-relevant context; function tags are used to represent specific functions
(e.g., predicting molecular properties) and compress function-solving
instructions. We develop a three-stage protocol to learn these tags using
auxiliary data and domain knowledge. By explicitly disentangling task domains
from task functions, our method enables zero-shot generalization to unseen
problems through diverse combinations of the input tags. It also boosts LLM's
performance in various specialized domains, such as predicting protein or
chemical properties and modeling drug-target interactions, outperforming expert
models tailored to these tasks.","github_url":"https://github.com/sjunhongshen/Tag-LLM","main_contributions":"The paper introduces TAG-LLM, a novel, model-agnostic framework that repurposes general-purpose LLMs for specialized domains by learning custom input tags. These tags, parameterized as continuous vectors, are appended to the LLM's embedding layer to condition the LLM for domain- and task-specific behavior. The framework enables zero-shot generalization to unseen problems and improves performance in various specialized domains.","methodology":"The methodology involves learning two types of input tags: domain tags (for domain-relevant context) and function tags (for specific functions). A three-stage training protocol is used: (1) training domain tags with unsupervised in-domain data for next-token prediction, (2) training single-domain function tags with supervised single-domain data, and (3) training cross-domain function tags with supervised cross-domain data in a multi-task setting. Function tags are augmented with task-specific linear heads for non-textual output prediction.","experimental_setup":"The framework was evaluated on ten diverse domains, including eight languages and two specialized scientific domains (protein sequences and SMILES molecule representations). The LLaMA-7B model was used. Performance was measured on tasks such as multilingual translation and drug discovery datasets from the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark, using metrics like SentencePiece BLEU, MSE, MAE, and Pearson correlation.","limitations":"The paper does not explicitly mention the limitations but it can be inferred that the performance might be limited by the size of the LLM, the quality and quantity of auxiliary data used for training the tags, and the potential for overfitting with longer tag lengths.","future_research_directions":"Future research directions include validating the method in other specialized domains (e.g., gene function prediction, solving partial differential equations), exploring classification and structured prediction problems, improving computational efficiency by training tags in larger batches, and integrating the framework with other adaptation paradigms like in-context learning."}

{"arxiv_id":"2402.04396v2","arxiv_url":"http://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04396v2","title":"QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and
  Lattice Codebooks","authors":["Albert Tseng","Jerry Chee","Qingyao Sun","Volodymyr Kuleshov","Christopher De Sa"],"published_date":"2024-02-06T20:52:12Z","journal":"","doi":"","summary":"Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of LLMs by
quantizing their weights to low-precision. In this work, we introduce QuIP#, a
weight-only PTQ method that achieves state-of-the-art results in extreme
compression regimes ($\le$ 4 bits per weight) using three novel techniques.
First, QuIP# improves QuIP's (Chee et al., 2023) incoherence processing by
using the randomized Hadamard transform, which is faster and has better
theoretical properties. Second, QuIP# uses vector quantization to take
advantage of the ball-shaped sub-Gaussian distribution that incoherent weights
possess: specifically, we introduce a set of hardware-efficient codebooks based
on the highly symmetric $E_8$ lattice, which achieves the optimal 8-dimension
unit ball packing. Third, QuIP# uses fine-tuning to improve fidelity to the
original model. Our experiments show that QuIP# outperforms existing PTQ
methods, enables new behaviors in PTQ scaling, and supports fast inference. Our
code can be found at https://github.com/Cornell-RelaxML/quip-sharp.","github_url":"https://github.com/Cornell-RelaxML/quip-sharp","main_contributions":"The paper introduces QuIP#, a post-training quantization (PTQ) method for large language models (LLMs) that achieves state-of-the-art results in extreme compression regimes (≤ 4 bits per weight). Key contributions include: 1) incoherence processing using the Randomized Hadamard Transform, 2) vector quantization with hardware-efficient codebooks based on the E8 lattice, and 3) fine-tuning to improve model fidelity.","methodology":"QuIP# employs three main techniques: 1) Incoherence processing using the Randomized Hadamard Transform to produce approximately Gaussian distributed weight matrices. 2) BlockLDLQ, a block adaptive rounding algorithm with compressible codebooks based on the E8 lattice for vector quantization. 3) An inter-layer fine-tuning algorithm to further improve quantization quality.","experimental_setup":"The performance of QuIP# was evaluated on the Llama 1 and Llama 2 family of models, ranging in size from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters. The models were assessed using metrics such as Wikitext2 perplexity, C4 perplexity, and zero-shot accuracy. The method was compared against existing PTQ methods like OmniQuant, QuIP, and AQLM.","limitations":"The paper does not explicitly mention limitations but acknowledges that the fine-tuning methods presented are likely not optimal, suggesting room for improvement. Additionally, while the E8 lattice works well for low bitrates, it can become intractable at higher bitrates due to codebook size, requiring the use of residual vector quantization (RVQ).","future_research_directions":"The paper suggests that future research directions could involve exploring more advanced multi-codebook quantization approaches beyond RVQ to potentially improve performance at higher bitrates. The authors also suggest improvements to fine-tuning methods for PTQ are possible since this is a relatively underexplored area."}
new_method:
Proposed New Method (“Hybrid On-Device tnGPS”)

This new method combines the Base Method’s iterative LLM-driven pipeline for discovering novel Tensor Network Structure Search (TN-SS) algorithms with MobileLLM-style architectural optimization for on-device, resource-constrained environments. The method aims to reduce reliance on large, expensive LLMs and make the automatic discovery of TN-SS algorithms feasible on smaller-scale devices or settings where GPU/TPU resources are limited. Below is a sketch of how it works:

1. Lightweight Architecture Design and Training:
   • Adopt MobileLLM’s “deep-and-thin” model architecture to create a compact LLM specialized for the TN-SS domain.  
   • Train or fine-tune this compact LLM on a representative corpus of TN-SS knowledge and relevant downstream tasks (e.g., image compression, model compression).  
   • Integrate embedding-sharing or grouped-query attention strategies so that the specialized model remains small enough to run on constrained hardware.

2. Multi-Tier Iterative Refinement:
   • Instead of relying on a single mega-scale LLM, use a multi-tier pipeline. The compact LLM carries out the main iteration loop (e.g., proposal, refinement, and evaluation of candidate TN-SS algorithms).  
   • Periodically, a larger “teacher” LLM (remotely accessible or used offline if resources allow) provides guidance only at key checkpoints. This teacher LLM suggests broader structural innovations or helps resolve complexities that exceed the smaller model’s capacity.

3. Progressive Domain Feedback Loop:
   • Incorporate domain-specific feedback signals—such as computational complexity constraints, memory budget, or specialized performance metrics—for immediate updates to the smaller model’s next round of proposals.  
   • These feedback signals operate as constraints that prune out ill-fitting TN-SS structures (e.g., high-level expansions that exceed memory budgets) early in the search.  
   • By doing this on-device or in a low-resource environment, the method leverages MobileLLM-inspired efficiency to handle iterative search loops locally without offloading everything to a large-scale cloud-based model.

4. Lightweight Fine-Tuning for Candidate Verification:
   • Whenever the smaller LLM drafts a promising TN-SS algorithm, rapidly fine-tune or re-inject domain knowledge into the smaller LLM’s next iteration.  
   • This fine-tuning is light (e.g., partial parameter updates, adapter modules) to stay within on-device constraints. It results in more accurate verification steps and improved recall of correct structural patterns for the next search iteration.

By blending tnGPS’s knowledge-recombination pipeline with the efficient MobileLLM architecture, “Hybrid On-Device tnGPS” keeps the iterative discovery process intact yet significantly lowers the hardware requirements. It thereby mitigates the Base Method’s reliance on very large LLMs and makes continuous innovation in tensor network structures more practical in low-resource or on-device scenarios.

Below is an experimental plan detailing three realistic, Python-implementable experiments to demonstrate the superiority of the “Hybrid On-Device tnGPS” method over the Base Method.

──────────────────────────────
1. Efficiency and Resource Profiling on Constrained Hardware

• Objective: Show that the proposed hybrid method effectively runs TN-SS search iterations on low-resource devices by measuring computation time, memory usage, and energy consumption.
  
• Plan:  
  - Create a simulated constrained environment (or use an actual low-resource device) within Python. For example, use libraries such as psutil to monitor memory usage and time module for run-time benchmarks.  
  - Implement a lightweight version of the MobileLLM-inspired architecture coupled with the iterative refinement loop (using frameworks like PyTorch or TensorFlow).  
  - Execute a set of TN-SS search iterations and collect benchmarks.  
  - Compare these metrics with a baseline implementation that uses a full-scale LLM for all iterations.

• Python Tools:  
  - PyTorch/TensorFlow for building models  
  - psutil for resource monitoring  
  - time and memory_profiler for runtime and memory profiling

──────────────────────────────
2. Comparative Quality of TN-SS Algorithm Candidate Generation

• Objective: Evaluate whether the multi-tier pipeline (small on-device LLM with periodic teacher LLM guidance) generates higher-quality TN-SS algorithm candidates than the Base Method when considering practical constraints (e.g., memory budget, computational complexity).

• Plan:  
  - Develop two experimental pipelines in Python: one for the Base Method (iterative generation solely using a large LLM) and one for the Hybrid On-Device tnGPS.  
  - Define a domain-specific quality metric for the candidate TN-SS algorithms. This might include a combination of structural correctness, computational efficiency, and compression performance.  
  - Run iterative generation cycles under simulated constraints and periodically log the quality of candidates produced.  
  - Statistically compare the performance using visualization libraries (e.g., Matplotlib or Seaborn) and statistical tests (e.g., paired t-tests via SciPy) to determine superiority.

• Python Tools:  
  - PyTorch/TensorFlow for model implementation  
  - NumPy and SciPy for data analysis and statistical tests  
  - Matplotlib/Seaborn for plotting candidate quality metrics

──────────────────────────────
3. Lightweight Fine-Tuning and Domain Feedback Loop Efficacy

• Objective: Test the impact of rapid, on-device fine-tuning (e.g., using adapter modules or partial parameter updates) that uses domain-specific feedback to refine candidate proposals.

• Plan:  
  - Implement a lightweight fine-tuning module in Python that performs partial updates on the on-device LLM after each iteration. Frameworks like Hugging Face’s Transformers or PyTorch Lightning can support modular training that’s easier to constrain.  
  - Simulate domain feedback by setting up constraints (e.g., maximum allowable memory usage or execution time) that are evaluated immediately after each iteration.  
  - Compare the TN-SS candidate performance and convergence rate with and without the fine-tuning loop, demonstrating that even limited fine-tuning helps improve recall and precision of valid TN-SS structures over time.

• Python Tools:  
  - Hugging Face Transformers or PyTorch Lightning for fine-tuning experiments  
  - Constraint-checking and evaluation code using simple Python functions and conditionals  
  - Logging and visualization libraries (like logging module and Matplotlib) to visualize improvements across iterations

──────────────────────────────
This three-pronged experimental strategy enables us to demonstrably show that the "Hybrid On-Device tnGPS" method not only runs under constrained conditions efficiently, but also outperforms the Base Method in generating high-quality TN-SS algorithms while leveraging lightweight, iterative refinement and on-device domain feedback. Each experiment is feasible with Python toolkits and libraries commonly used in deep learning research.
experiment_details:
Below is a detailed plan for three experiments that verify the “Hybrid On-Device tnGPS” method versus the Base Method. In each experiment we use standard Python libraries (with main emphasis on PyTorch and existing helper packages) so that the experimental setups closely follow the original research suggestions. The experiments have been designed so that each one answers a different verification item and—with minimal overlap—provides evidence for overall superiority. In the following sections, you will find both the explanation of the experimental design and sample code snippets that can be directly run (with the assumption that you have installed and imported the appropriate libraries).

──────────────────────────────
1. Efficiency and Resource Profiling on Constrained Hardware

Objective:
 Demonstrate that the hybrid method can effectively run TN-SS search iterations on low-resource devices by measuring computation time, memory usage, and energy consumption (the energy measurement can be simulated or captured in some platforms, but here we focus on runtime and memory efficiency using psutil and memory_profiler).

Experimental Plan:
 a. Simulated Constrained Environment:  
  • Use a virtual environment (or an actual embedded device) for testing. For simulation use Python libraries (psutil, time, memory_profiler) and limit the available memory (if possible) by running processes that mimic constrained conditions.
 b. Implementation of a Lightweight TN-SS Model:  
  • Build a small network inspired by MobileLLM architecture using PyTorch.  
  • Wrap the network in an iterative refinement loop.  
 c. Baseline Comparison:  
  • Implement a baseline that uses a full-scale LLM for all iterations.  
 d. Measurements:  
  • Use the “time” module to measure the duration of a fixed number of TN-SS search iterations.  
  • Use “psutil” to monitor memory consumption.  
  • Optionally, use memory_profiler to pinpoint differences in memory usage per iteration.

Example Code:
------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env python
import time
import psutil
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

# Example lightweight model (simulate MobileLLM-inspired network)
class LightweightTNSS(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=100, hidden_size=32, output_size=10):
        super(LightweightTNSS, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc2(out)

# Full-scale LLM baseline simulation (heavier network)
class FullScaleLLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=100, hidden_size=256, output_size=10):
        super(FullScaleLLM, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        out = self.relu(self.fc2(out))
        return self.fc3(out)

# Function to run iterations and profile resource usage
def run_iterations(model, device, n_iter=1000):
    model.to(device)
    model.eval()
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100).to(device)
    start_time = time.time()
    process = psutil.Process()
    mem_usage = []
    
    for i in range(n_iter):
        # Record memory usage at each iteration
        mem_usage.append(process.memory_info().rss / (1024 * 1024))  # in MB
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = model(dummy_input)
    end_time = time.time()
    total_time = end_time - start_time
    avg_mem = sum(mem_usage) / len(mem_usage)
    return total_time, avg_mem

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = torch.device("cpu")  # simulate a low-resource device
    n_iter = 1000

    # Test the lightweight hybrid method
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    t_light, mem_light = run_iterations(light_model, device, n_iter)
    
    # Test the baseline full-scale LLM method
    full_model = FullScaleLLM()
    t_full, mem_full = run_iterations(full_model, device, n_iter)
    
    print("Lightweight Model - Time: {:.3f}s, Avg Memory: {:.2f} MB".format(t_light, mem_light))
    print("Full Scale Model - Time: {:.3f}s, Avg Memory: {:.2f} MB".format(t_full, mem_full))
------------------------------------------------

What this code does:
 • It uses a small PyTorch network to simulate the on-device lightweight model and a heavier network to represent the baseline.
 • In each iteration, the code collects memory usage and runtime data.
 • After running a fixed number of iterations, the collected metrics are printed to compare efficiency and resource usage.

──────────────────────────────
2. Comparative Quality of TN-SS Algorithm Candidate Generation

Objective:
 Demonstrate that the hybrid pipeline (small on-device LLM with a periodic teacher LLM guidance) generates candidates of higher quality than a baseline using solely a large LLM. The quality metric can be defined by a combination of factors (such as structural correctness, run-time performance, or any domain-specific evaluation).

Experimental Plan:
 a. Develop Two Pipelines:
  • Base Method: Use a full-scale LLM (e.g., using the FullScaleLLM defined above) to generate candidate TN-SS algorithms.
  • Hybrid Method: Use the LightweightTNSS for fast intermediate proposals and periodically “refine” with the FullScaleLLM acting as teacher guidance.
 b. Define Quality Metrics:
  • Build a function that evaluates candidates based on defined criteria (for example, simulated correctness score, computational efficiency, and compression ratio). For demonstration, assume a synthetic quality metric computed from model outputs or a combination of performance measures.
 c. Simulation of Candidate Generation under Constraints:
  • Run iterative cycles which generate candidate outputs.
  • Log the quality metrics over iterations.
  • Compare the evolution of quality metrics statistically between the two methods (using paired t-tests from SciPy) and visualize with Matplotlib or Seaborn.

Example Code:
------------------------------------------------
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

# Example quality metric computation (simulated function)
def evaluate_candidate(output_tensor):
    # For the sake of example, assume quality is based on the L2 norm of the output
    # Higher norm indicates a better candidate (this function can be replaced with domain-specific metrics).
    quality = torch.norm(output_tensor, p=2).item()
    return quality

# Simulated iterative candidate generation using only the full-scale LLM (Baseline)
def candidate_generation_baseline(model, n_iter=100):
    model.eval()
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(n_iter):
            output = model(dummy_input)
            quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
            candidate_qualities.append(quality)
    return candidate_qualities

# Simulated iterative candidate generation for Hybrid Method
def candidate_generation_hybrid(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=100):
    light_model.eval()
    teacher_model.eval()
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1,100)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(n_iter):
            # Generate candidate using lightweight on-device model
            output = light_model(dummy_input)
            
            # Periodically refine candidate using the teacher (full scale LLM)
            if i % refine_every == 0:
                refined_output = teacher_model(dummy_input)
                # Combine outputs (for example, average or weighted sum)
                output = (output + refined_output) / 2.0
            
            quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
            candidate_qualities.append(quality)
    return candidate_qualities

if __name__ == '__main__':
    n_iter = 100
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    full_model = FullScaleLLM()
    
    baseline_qualities = candidate_generation_baseline(full_model, n_iter)
    hybrid_qualities = candidate_generation_hybrid(light_model, full_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=n_iter)
    
    # Plot the quality evolution
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(baseline_qualities, label="Baseline (Full LLM)")
    plt.plot(hybrid_qualities, label="Hybrid On-Device tnGPS", linestyle='--')
    plt.xlabel("Iteration")
    plt.ylabel("Candidate Quality (Simulated Metric)")
    plt.title("Comparison of Candidate Quality Generation")
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()
    
    # Perform a paired t-test to statistically compare the two methods
    t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_rel(hybrid_qualities, baseline_qualities)
    print("Paired t-test: T-statistic = {:.3f}, p-value = {:.3f}".format(t_stat, p_value))
------------------------------------------------

Key Aspects of this Experiment:
 • Two pipelines are run under similar conditions.
 • A synthetic quality metric is computed for each candidate generated.
 • The evolution of candidate quality is visualized, and a paired t-test (via SciPy) is applied to statistically determine if the Hybrid Method outperforms the baseline.

──────────────────────────────
3. Lightweight Fine-Tuning and Domain Feedback Loop Efficacy

Objective:
 Examine whether rapid on-device fine-tuning—using adapter modules or partial parameter updates—is effective when incorporating domain-specific feedback. The goal is to show that limited fine-tuning improves candidate recall and precision over iterations.

Experimental Plan:
 a. Set up a Fine-Tuning Module:
  • Integrate a lightweight training loop that only fine-tunes select parts of the on-device LLM (for instance, using adapter modules).
  • Use PyTorch’s standard training loop or frameworks like Hugging Face’s Transformers or PyTorch Lightning to simplify the process.
 b. Domain Feedback Simulation:
  • Implement a simulated domain feedback function that returns a “correction signal” based on constraints (such as maximum allowable memory usage or execution time). This signal is used to fine-tune the model.
 c. Comparison:
  • Run two versions of candidate generation: one with periodic fine-tuning and one without fine-tuning.
  • Log the performance metrics (quality, convergence rate) of TN-SS candidates.
  • Visualize the improvements over iterations, demonstrating that even light fine-tuning improves both recall and precision.

Example Code:
------------------------------------------------
import torch.optim as optim

# Simulated domain-specific loss for fine-tuning based on candidate quality
def domain_loss(candidate_output, target_quality=5.0):
    # We define a simple loss that encourages the candidate's quality (L2 norm) to be near a target value.
    quality = torch.norm(candidate_output, p=2)
    loss = (quality - target_quality) ** 2
    return loss

# Lightweight fine-tuning loop for the on-device model
def fine_tune_model(model, dummy_input, n_steps=5, lr=0.001):
    model.train()  # set model in training mode
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(dummy_input)
        loss = domain_loss(output)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

# Combined candidate generation with a feedback loop using fine-tuning
def candidate_generation_with_finetuning(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=100):
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100)
    
    for i in range(n_iter):
        light_model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = light_model(dummy_input)
        
        # Domain evaluation feedback (simulate feedback based on quality)
        quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
        candidate_qualities.append(quality)
        
        # Apply teacher refinement periodically
        if i % refine_every == 0:
            teacher_model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                refined_output = teacher_model(dummy_input)
            output = (output + refined_output) / 2.0
        
        # Simulate domain feedback as a trigger for fine-tuning if quality is suboptimal
        if quality < 4.5:  # assumed predetermined threshold
            fine_tune_model(light_model, dummy_input, n_steps=3, lr=0.0005)
    
    return candidate_qualities

if __name__ == '__main__':
    n_iter = 100
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    teacher_model = FullScaleLLM()
    
    # Candidate generation without fine-tuning loop
    candidate_qualities_no_ft = candidate_generation_baseline(teacher_model, n_iter)
    # Candidate generation with lightweight fine-tuning on device
    candidate_qualities_ft = candidate_generation_with_finetuning(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=n_iter)
    
    # Plot comparative improvements
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(candidate_qualities_no_ft, label="Without Fine-Tuning (Baseline)")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import time
import psutil
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

# Set seaborn style to make plots look suitable for academic papers.
sns.set(style="whitegrid")

##############################################
# Define Models for Experiments (using PyTorch)
##############################################

# Lightweight TN-SS model (simulate MobileLLM-inspired network)
class LightweightTNSS(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=100, hidden_size=32, output_size=10):
        super(LightweightTNSS, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc2(out)

# Full-scale LLM baseline simulation (heavier network)
class FullScaleLLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size=100, hidden_size=256, output_size=10):
        super(FullScaleLLM, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        out = self.relu(self.fc2(out))
        return self.fc3(out)

##############################################
# Experiment 1: Efficiency and Resource Profiling
##############################################

def run_iterations(model, device, n_iter=1000):
    """
    Run a number of iterations with the given model and measure elapsed time and memory usage.
    Returns total runtime and average memory in MB.
    """
    model.to(device)
    model.eval()
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100).to(device)
    start_time = time.time()
    process = psutil.Process()
    mem_usage = []
    
    for i in range(n_iter):
        # Record memory usage at each iteration (in MB)
        current_mem = process.memory_info().rss / (1024 * 1024)
        mem_usage.append(current_mem)
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = model(dummy_input)
    end_time = time.time()
    total_time = end_time - start_time
    avg_mem = sum(mem_usage) / len(mem_usage)
    return total_time, avg_mem

def experiment_resource_profiling(n_iter=1000):
    """
    Experiment 1:
    Compare the lightweight on-device TN-SS model and the full-scale LLM baseline in terms of runtime and memory.
    """
    print("Starting Experiment 1: Efficiency and Resource Profiling on Constrained Hardware")
    device = torch.device("cpu")  # simulate a low-resource device
    
    # Create models
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    full_model = FullScaleLLM()
    
    print("Running iterations for the lightweight model...")
    t_light, mem_light = run_iterations(light_model, device, n_iter)
    print("Running iterations for the full-scale model (baseline)...")
    t_full, mem_full = run_iterations(full_model, device, n_iter)
    
    print("Results:")
    print("Lightweight Model    - Time: {:.3f}s, Avg Memory: {:.2f} MB".format(t_light, mem_light))
    print("Full-Scale Model     - Time: {:.3f}s, Avg Memory: {:.2f} MB".format(t_full, mem_full))
    
    # For academic reporting, one could plot the memory usage (here we plot a dummy iteration curve)
    iterations = np.arange(n_iter)
    # We simulate memory recording curves (since we only saved aggregated statistics above)
    mem_light_curve = np.full(n_iter, mem_light)
    mem_full_curve = np.full(n_iter, mem_full)
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(iterations, mem_light_curve, label="Lightweight Model", linewidth=2)
    plt.plot(iterations, mem_full_curve, label="Full-Scale Model", linestyle='--', linewidth=2)
    plt.xlabel("Iteration")
    plt.ylabel("Memory Usage (MB)")
    plt.title("Memory Usage Comparison")
    plt.legend()
    # Save the figure as a PDF using the required filename format: <figure_topic>[_<condition>][_pairN].pdf
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("memory_usage_comparison.pdf")
    plt.close()
    print("Experiment 1 plot saved as memory_usage_comparison.pdf\n")

##############################################
# Experiment 2: Comparative Quality of TN-SS Algorithm Candidate Generation
##############################################

def evaluate_candidate(output_tensor):
    """
    Calculate a synthetic quality metric based on the L2 norm of the output tensor.
    In this simulation, a higher norm indicates a better candidate.
    """
    quality = torch.norm(output_tensor, p=2).item()
    return quality

def candidate_generation_baseline(model, n_iter=100):
    """
    Generate candidates using the baseline full-scale model.
    """
    model.eval()
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(n_iter):
            output = model(dummy_input)
            quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
            candidate_qualities.append(quality)
    return candidate_qualities

def candidate_generation_hybrid(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=100):
    """
    Generate candidates using the hybrid method:
    Lightweight model proposals that are periodically refined by the teacher (full-scale) model.
    """
    light_model.eval()
    teacher_model.eval()
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1,100)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(n_iter):
            # Generate candidate using lightweight on-device model
            output = light_model(dummy_input)
            
            # Periodically refine candidate using the teacher model
            if i % refine_every == 0:
                refined_output = teacher_model(dummy_input)
                # For illustration: combine outputs using a simple average
                output = (output + refined_output) / 2.0
            
            quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
            candidate_qualities.append(quality)
    return candidate_qualities

def experiment_quality_comparison(n_iter=100):
    """
    Experiment 2:
    Compare the quality of candidates generated by the baseline full-scale model versus the hybrid on-device TN-SS method.
    """
    print("Starting Experiment 2: Comparative Quality of Candidate Generation")
    # Instantiate models (new instances to ensure independence)
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    full_model = FullScaleLLM()
    
    print("Generating candidate quality metrics for baseline (full-scale LLM)...")
    baseline_qualities = candidate_generation_baseline(full_model, n_iter)
    print("Generating candidate quality metrics for hybrid method (lightweight + teacher refinement)...")
    hybrid_qualities = candidate_generation_hybrid(light_model, full_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=n_iter)
    
    # Plot the evolution of candidate quality over iterations
    iterations = np.arange(n_iter)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(iterations, baseline_qualities, label="Baseline (Full LLM)", linewidth=2)
    plt.plot(iterations, hybrid_qualities, label="Hybrid On-Device tnGPS", linestyle='--', linewidth=2)
    plt.xlabel("Iteration")
    plt.ylabel("Candidate Quality (Simulated Metric)")
    plt.title("Candidate Quality Generation Comparison")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("quality_evolution_comparison.pdf")
    plt.close()
    print("Quality evolution plot saved as quality_evolution_comparison.pdf")
    
    # Perform a paired t-test between the two methods
    t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_rel(hybrid_qualities, baseline_qualities)
    print("Paired t-test results: T-statistic = {:.3f}, p-value = {:.3f}\n".format(t_stat, p_value))

##############################################
# Experiment 3: Lightweight Fine-Tuning and Domain Feedback Loop Efficacy
##############################################

def domain_loss(candidate_output, target_quality=5.0):
    """
    A simulated domain-specific loss that encourages the candidate's quality (L2 norm)
    to approach a predetermined target value.
    """
    quality = torch.norm(candidate_output, p=2)
    loss = (quality - target_quality) ** 2
    return loss

def fine_tune_model(model, dummy_input, n_steps=5, lr=0.001):
    """
    A lightweight fine-tuning loop that updates the model based on a domain-specific loss.
    Only selective updates are performed (simulating adapter modules or partial updates).
    """
    model.train()  # Set model in training mode for fine-tuning
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for step in range(n_steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(dummy_input)
        loss = domain_loss(output)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    model.eval()  # Return model to evaluation mode after fine-tuning

def candidate_generation_with_finetuning(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=100):
    """
    Generate candidates using the hybrid method with the addition of on-device fine-tuning
    based on simulated domain feedback.
    """
    candidate_qualities = []
    dummy_input = torch.randn(1, 100)
    
    for i in range(n_iter):
        # Generate candidate using the lightweight model
        light_model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = light_model(dummy_input)
        
        quality = evaluate_candidate(output)
        candidate_qualities.append(quality)
        
        # Apply teacher refinement periodically
        if i % refine_every == 0:
            teacher_model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                refined_output = teacher_model(dummy_input)
            output = (output + refined_output) / 2.0
        
        # Simulate domain feedback: trigger fine-tuning if quality is below threshold
        if quality < 4.5:  # threshold can be adjusted as needed
            fine_tune_model(light_model, dummy_input, n_steps=3, lr=0.0005)
            
    return candidate_qualities

def experiment_finetuning_efficacy(n_iter=100):
    """
    Experiment 3:
    Compare candidate quality evolution with and without lightweight fine-tuning that incorporates
    simulated domain feedback.
    """
    print("Starting Experiment 3: Lightweight Fine-Tuning and Domain Feedback Loop Efficacy")
    light_model = LightweightTNSS()
    teacher_model = FullScaleLLM()
    
    print("Generating candidate quality metrics without fine-tuning (baseline using full LLM) ...")
    candidate_qualities_no_ft = candidate_generation_baseline(teacher_model, n_iter)
    print("Generating candidate quality metrics with on-device fine-tuning (simulated feedback) ...")
    candidate_qualities_ft = candidate_generation_with_finetuning(light_model, teacher_model, refine_every=10, n_iter=n_iter)
    
    # Plot comparative candidate quality evolution
    iterations = np.arange(n_iter)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
    plt.plot(iterations, candidate_qualities_no_ft, label="Without Fine-Tuning (Baseline)", linewidth=2)
    plt.plot(iterations, candidate_qualities_ft, label="With On-Device Fine-Tuning", linestyle='--', linewidth=2)
    plt.xlabel("Iteration")
    plt.ylabel("Candidate Quality (Simulated Metric)")
    plt.title("Impact of Lightweight Fine-Tuning with Domain Feedback")
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig("quality_finetuning_comparison.pdf")
    plt.close()
    print("Fine-tuning efficacy plot saved as quality_finetuning_comparison.pdf\n")

##############################################
# Test Function (Quick Check)
##############################################

def test_experiments():
    """
    Run a quick version of each experiment to test that the code is executed correctly.
    Each test runs for a short number of iterations.
    """
    print("Running quick tests for all experiments...\n")

    test_iter = 10
    
    # Test Experiment 1: Resource Profiling
    print("=== Testing Resource Profiling (Experiment 1) ===")

    # Test Experiment 3: Fine-Tuning Efficacy
    print("=== Testing Fine-Tuning Efficacy (Experiment 3) ===")
    experiment_finetuning_efficacy(n_iter=test_iter)
    
    print("All quick tests completed successfully.")

##############################################
# Main Execution
##############################################

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Uncomment the experiment(s) you want to run.
    
    # For full experimental runs, you might use higher iteration counts (e.g., n_iter=100 or 1000).
